In [[mathematics]], the '''Kummer–Vandiver conjecture''', or '''Vandiver conjecture''', states that a [[prime number|prime]] <math>p</math> does not divide the [[class number (number theory)|class number]] <math>h_K</math> of the maximal real [[field extension|subfield]] <math>K = \mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p)^+</math> of the <math>p</math>-th [[cyclotomic field]]. The [[conjecture]] was first made by [[Ernst Kummer]], on 28 December 1849 and 24 April 1853 in letters to [[Leopold Kronecker]],{{sfnp|Kummer|1975|pp=84, 93, 123–124}} and independently rediscovered around 1920 by [[Philipp Furtwängler]] and [[Harry Vandiver]].{{sfnp|Vandiver|1946|loc=p. 576}}

As of 2011, there is no particularly strong evidence either for or against the conjecture and it is unclear whether it is true or false, though it is likely that [[counterexample]]s are very rare.

==Background==

The class number <math>h</math> of the cyclotomic field  <math>\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p)</math> is a product of two [[integer]]s <math>h_1</math> and <math>h_2</math>, called the first and second factors of the class number, where <math>h_2</math> is the class number of the maximal real subfield <math>K = \mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p)^+</math> of the <math>p</math>-th cyclotomic field. The first factor <math>h_1</math> is well understood and can be computed easily in terms of [[Bernoulli number]]s, and is usually rather large. The second factor <math>h_2</math> is not well understood and is hard to compute explicitly, and in the cases when it has been computed it is usually small.

Kummer showed that if a prime <math>p</math> does not divide the class number <math>h</math>, then [[Fermat's Last Theorem]] holds for exponent <math>p</math>.

The Kummer–Vandiver conjecture states that <math>p</math> does not divide the second factor <math>h_2</math>. Kummer showed that if <math>p</math> divides the second factor, then it also divides the first factor. In particular the Kummer–Vandiver conjecture holds for [[regular prime]]s (those for which <math>p</math> does not divide the first factor).

==Evidence for and against the Kummer–Vandiver conjecture==

Kummer verified the Kummer–Vandiver conjecture for <math>p</math> less than 200, and Vandiver extended this to <math>p</math> less than 600. [[Joe Buhler|Buhler]], [[Richard Crandall|Crandall]] et al. verified it for ''p'' < 12000000.{{sfnp|Buhler|Crandall|Ernvall|Metsänkylä|2001}} Buhler and Harvey extended this to primes less than 163000000,{{sfnp|Buhler|Harvey|2011}} and Hart, Harvey, and Ong extended this to primes less than 2<sup>31</sup>.{{sfnp|Hart|Harvey|Ong|2017}}

[[Lawrence C. Washington|Washington]] describes an informal probability argument,{{sfnp|Washington|1996|p=158}} based on rather dubious assumptions{{clarify|date=July 2026}} about the equidistribution of class numbers modulo <math>p</math>, suggesting that the number of primes less than <math>x</math> that are exceptions to the Kummer–Vandiver conjecture might grow like <math>(\log\log x)/2</math>. This grows extremely slowly, and suggests that the computer calculations do not provide much evidence for Vandiver's conjecture: for example, the probability argument (combined with the calculations for small primes) suggests that one should only expect about 1 counterexample in the first 10<sup>100</sup> primes, suggesting that it is unlikely any counterexample will be found by further brute force searches even if there are an infinite number of exceptions.

[[René Schoof|Schoof]] gave conjectural calculations of the class numbers of real cyclotomic fields for primes up to 10000, which strongly suggest that the class numbers are not randomly distributed mod <math>p</math>.{{sfnp|Schoof|2003}} They tend to be quite small and are often just <math>1</math>. For example, assuming the [[generalized Riemann hypothesis]], the class number of the real cyclotomic field for the prime <math>p</math> is <math>1</math> for <math>p<163</math>, and divisible by <math>4</math> for <math>p=163</math>. This suggests that Washington's informal probability argument against the conjecture may be misleading.

Mihăilescu gave a refined version of Washington's heuristic argument, suggesting that the Kummer–Vandiver conjecture is probably true.{{sfnp|Mihăilescu|2012}}

==Consequences of the Kummer–Vandiver conjecture==
Kurihara showed that the conjecture is equivalent to a statement in the [[algebraic K-theory]] of the integers, namely that  <math>K_n(\Z)=0</math> whenever <math>n</math> is a multiple of <math>4</math>.{{sfnp|Kurihara|1992}}{{sfnp|Ghate|2000}} In fact, from the Kummer–Vandiver conjecture and the [[norm residue isomorphism theorem]] follows a full conjectural calculation of the <math>K</math>-groups for all values of <math>n</math>; see [[Quillen–Lichtenbaum conjecture]] for details.
